name: Oral rehydration salts (ORS)
short: Case reports: fatal high blood sodium after an ORS packet was wrongly made up, and in a young child after a wrongly made salt solution. Cholera trials: low sodium more often on reduced-osmolarity ORS.
text: Oral rehydration solution (ORS), described in the cited reviews as a glucose-based solution containing sodium, is used to treat dehydration; these data come mainly from children and adults with diarrhoea or cholera, not from people with POTS; the POTS abstracts on the POTS page do not list the ingredients of the salts used, though one names a reduced-osmolarity formula and another compares two formulas (ORS I and ORS III). Preparation errors: a 2000 report of two infants with severe salt poisoning describes one of two young girls (aged 20 and 7 months; the abstract does not say which) who had seizures, a clotting disorder and a clot in a brain venous sinus after a mistake in preparing salt-saturated water as an oral rehydration solution; both children in the report (the other after salt was added to yoghurt by mistake) developed brain death. A 2010 report from India, titled as acute salt poisoning due to different ORS packet sizes, discusses two patients, whose ages the abstract does not give: one developed salt poisoning from improper dilution and recovered after rapid correction, and in the other improper reconstitution led to hypernatraemia (high blood sodium) and death. The report explains that some companies in India make smaller packets than the standard one and that, out of confusion, some prescribers advise dissolving the standard packet in the amount of water meant for a smaller packet. In Egypt, as ORS prepared from packets came into wider use, hypernatraemia (blood sodium above 150 mmol/l) among children admitted with dehydration to one Cairo hospital rose between 1980 and 1984, peaking at 49% of 222 inpatient children in 1984 (19% severe); among at least 1,000 dehydrated outpatients surveyed each year from 1986, it had fallen to around 10% by 1989 (2% severe). The authors report that the rise and fall coincided with increasing use of ORS and then with mothers' increasing ability to mix the solution correctly, and that hypernatraemia was positively related to the quantity of ORS taken, among other factors such as the severity of dehydration. On the other side, in a review of children under 15 admitted to a Bangladesh hospital with diarrhoea and hypernatraemia, treatment with ORS alone, or ORS after intravenous fluid when needed, was associated with a lower risk of death in a logistic regression analysis. Blood sodium: in a Cochrane review of 7 trials (718 participants) in people with cholera, biochemical hyponatraemia (blood sodium below 130 mmol/L) was more common with reduced-osmolarity ORS than with standard ORS (relative risk 1.67; 4 trials, 465 participants), severe hyponatraemia was not significantly more common, and no trial reported symptomatic hyponatraemia or death; the authors advise caution where patient monitoring is difficult. In children admitted to hospital with diarrhoea, a Cochrane review found that reduced-osmolarity ORS led to fewer unscheduled intravenous infusions and less vomiting than the standard WHO solution, with no additional risk of hyponatraemia; a 2024 review notes that the lower-osmolarity solution was developed because of concerns about sodium levels and cases of hypernatraemia (high blood sodium) with the standard formula. In a randomised comparison of two oral rehydration salt formulas in children with neurally mediated syncope, including POTS (27 and 49 children), serum electrolytes did not differ significantly before and after treatment in either group. The other POTS studies on the POTS page report symptom or test outcomes without adverse-event data, and in one experimental study in 10 children with POTS and 15 controls, comparing ORS with saline infusion during a controlled orthostatic challenge, the authors describe ORS as safe without giving adverse-event data. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
